newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Scuffles, apathy greet Hong Kong's future leader.
newsitem.headline: Scuffles, apathy greet Hong Kong's future leader.

text.p: Scuffles, anger and plain apathy greeted the landslide victory of Tung Chee-hwa after an elite gathering on Wednesday chose the shipping magnate to be Hong Kong's leader when the British pull out next year.
While several business conglomerates congratulated Tung in splashy afternoon newspaper supplements, pro-democracy activists decried his victory as the death of law and freedom in the territory.
A 400-strong Selection Committee assembled by Beijing picked the 59-year-old businessman by an overwhelming vote of 340 to replace British governor Chris Patten next July 1.
Tung's closest rival and former Hong Kong chief justice Ti-Liang Yang got only 42, and third-placed Peter Woo just 36.
A sense of resignation marked the reactions of some citizens. "He got 320 votes? Well, I don't care. What power do I have to resist if I don't like it," clerk Raymond Chan said.
"It's just a sham, just a show China is putting on for the world. If it's a true election it would be one-man, one-vote," said Wah Pak, a 76-year-old retiree.
"I think it's the death of Hong Kong. Tung has not said one single thing that's different from China, he has so far not shown any independence of mind," a Hong Kong journalist said.
Some commuters took no interest when asked to comment, apathetically burying their heads in the racing pages of their newspapers.

As the elite committee gathered to decide who should run Hong Kong, more than 40 pro-democracy protesters scuffled with riot police and set fire to a mock ancient Chinese-style gray arched tomb, symbolising the death of democracy.

One of Hong Kong's best-known pro-democracy politicians, Emily Lau, together with 28 others, was dragged away and arrested by police after lying down on a road to protest China's methods of choosing the future leader.
Upon hearing the news of Tung's selection, protesters unfurled two large and colourful scrolls criticising the selection process and condemning the result.
"Oppose small-circle selection, we want the election of the chief executive by all Hong Kong people," they said.
